This division relates to the Policy _[For limiting availability of welfare payments](/policies/34)_. The majority voted against an amendment to the original motion, introduced by Greens Senator Sarah Hanson-Young. The original motion was "that the bill be now read a second time"(Read more about the stages that a bill must pass through to become law [here](http://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). ) to which Senator Hanson-Young moved the following amendment: _At the end of the motion, add:_ _but the Senate is of the opinion that, rather than punishing families, revenue should be raised from big miners, bankers and polluters through:_ _(a) applying a 'public insurance' levy on the big four banks that are too big to fail;_ _(b) removing fossil fuel subsidised fuel for big mining companies;_ _(c) retaining the billions in revenue from the carbon price;_ _(d) implementing the original super profits mining tax;_ _(e) imposing a millionaires tax;_ _(f) taxing discretionary trusts as corporations; and_ _(g) imposing a levy on thermal coal imports exports._ Because the majority voted against this amendment, it was unsuccessful _Background to the bill_ The [bill](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r5271) was introduced primarily to amend the [A New Tax System (Family Assistance) Act 1999](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsaa1999357/) in order to: - maintain the indexation pause on the [Child Care Rebate](http://www.humanservices.gov.au/customer/services/centrelink/child-care-rebate) (CCR) limit at $7500 for three years from 1 July 2014; and - maintain the [Child Care Benefit](http://www.humanservices.gov.au/customer/services/centrelink/child-care-benefit) (CCB) income thresholds at the amounts applicable as at 30 June 2014 for three years from 1 July 2014. Normally, the CCR limit and CCB income test thresholds are indexed on an annual basis to the Consumer Price Index (CPI).

Introduced the Family Assistance Legislation Amendment (Child Care Measures) Bill 2014, freezing childcare benefit thresholds and the $7,500 rebate cap to save $230 million, and said an independent review found Labor's Early Years Quality Fund would have benefited less than 30 per cent of long day care workers before redirecting over $200 million to broader professional development.

Moved an amendment opposing the Child Care Measures Bill, arguing the government's paid parental leave scheme offers $50,000 cheques to millionaires while cutting childcare benefit for families earning as little as $42,000, and citing $230 million in cuts that the department says will affect around 500,000 families.

Argued the bill will strip $230 million from childcare benefit assistance relied on by over 889,000 families, said research shows every one per cent rise in childcare fees cuts mothers' workforce participation by 0.7 per cent, and noted 180 early childhood educators are leaving the underpaid sector every week.

Argued in support of the Child Care Measures Bill, detailing net savings of $105.8 million from freezing the childcare rebate and $230.4 million from freezing the childcare benefit, and said Labor had promised 260 new childcare centres but delivered only 38.

Defended the Family Assistance Legislation Amendment (Child Care Measures) Bill 2014, which freezes the $7,500 childcare rebate limit and childcare benefit income thresholds for three years to save $230 million, saying childcare fees had risen 50 per cent nationally during Labor's six years in government.

Opposed the Family Assistance Legislation Amendment (Child Care Measures) Bill 2014, saying it would strip $230 million from means-tested childcare benefits affecting 889,000 families, and that 74,000 families would reach the childcare rebate cut-off in 2014 alone.

Opposed the Family Assistance Legislation Amendment (Child Care Measures) Bill 2014, saying it would cut $336 million from childcare support and leave over 500,000 families worse off, and cited a Grattan Institute study estimating Australia's economy could be $35 billion better off if it matched Canada's childcare-driven workforce participation.

Opposed the Family Assistance child care bill, citing Goodstart research that children who miss preschool are 50 per cent more likely to be developmentally vulnerable, and calculated the bill's $76.9 million saving is only about 1.5 per cent of what the government's Paid Parental Leave scheme would cost in a year.

Opposed the Family Assistance child care bill, citing Early Childhood Australia modelling that a family earning $60,000 with one child in care would be $1,800 a year worse off by 2016-17, and described the threat to Nikinpa Aboriginal Child and Family Centre in his Charlton electorate from a $78 million annual cut to Indigenous child and family centres.

Said the government is increasing overall childcare assistance to $28½ billion over four years for about a million families, defended maintaining childcare benefit thresholds and pausing the childcare rebate limit at $7,500 per child for three more years as a Labor-originated measure, and said childcare fees rose 53 per cent under the previous government.

This bill is one of a package that introduces a temporary budget repair levy for three years, starting in the 2014-15 financial year, as extra income tax on individuals.
The levy would be added to tax rates that are tied to the top personal marginal rate and to the Medicare levy, to keep the system fair and reduce avoidance.
The levy rate is two per cent of taxable income above $180,000, with no levy for income at or below that amount unless integrity rules apply.
Introduces a three-year temporary budget repair levy on individuals.
Aligns certain tax rates with the new levy to preserve fairness and prevent avoidance.
Ensures higher-income earners contribute more to budget repair.
Australian resident and foreign resident individuals with taxable income over $180,000.

Christine Milne I move: _At the end of the motion, add:_ _but the Senate calls on the government to:_ _(a) extend the provisions of the levy beyond the 2016-17 financial year, making the levy permanent; and_ _(b) guarantee that no tax cuts will be made, or promised, for the top income tax bracket, prior to the 2016 election._ In other words, no tax cut, or promise of one, is permitted before the 2016 election. That would test the mettle of this. If you are serious about a permanent change for those who earn more than $180,000, you would have no concerns at all about supporting this amendment. I call on both the government and the Labor Party to support this amendment. We are not going to let the government off the hook with their temporary levy. We are not going to stand by and watch what is going to happen-that is, everybody else suffers while the rich get ready to organise themselves to not pay it, to minimise their income, and get ready for the tax cut in 2016. At a recent Senate hearing Senator Cormann said: _We are very conscious of the fact that high-income earners already do a lot of the heavy lifting when it comes to contributing to Commonwealth revenue. But in the context of this budget we decided and judged that it was necessary to ask everyone across the community to make a contribution, including asking high-income earners to make an additional effort on top of the significant effort that they are already making._ But the Grattan Institute made it clear that 'it does not share the pain very effectively as it will only have a short-term impact on high-income earners; and, by contrast, the spending cuts will have a disproportionately large effect on lower income earners and they are permanent'. And Saul Eslake made the point that 'it will encourage at least some higher income households to take more active steps to engage in tax minimisation or avoidance activities, including by making greater use of the myriad provisions in the income tax system which off

Criticized the budget's $30 billion cut to education and its plan to push people under 25 from Newstart onto the lower youth allowance, a cut of at least $48 a week or almost $2,500 a year, and warned nearly 600,000 Queensland pensioners' concessions are at risk from cuts to the states.

Argued this bill represents another broken promise on tax, cited NATSEM modelling that the poorest fifth of families with children will see a five per cent cut to disposable income against 0.3 per cent for the most affluent fifth, and recounted a distressed pensioner constituent with chronic leukaemia worried about affording her monthly medical treatment.

Detailed feedback from her Indi budget impact tour, said the levy will raise $3.1 billion by taxing the 2.3 per cent of Australians earning over $180,000, and moved an amendment to extend the levy to 2020 to 2021 so the burden is shared more fairly.

Criticised the budget's broken promises, said the government's $80 billion cut to education and health includes scrapping the Australia Network at a cost of $200 million to the ABC over eight years, and said changing the pension indexation method would leave a pensioner about $1,500 a year worse off had it applied over the past four years.

Argued the levy is necessary given the nation's $12 billion annual interest bill, equivalent to $1 billion a month, and warned that if unchecked, debt reaching $667 billion would push interest payments to $3 billion a month.

Defended the temporary budget repair levy raising the top marginal tax rate from 45 to 47 per cent on incomes above $180,000 from 1 July 2014 to 30 June 2017, noting that combined with other levies this would give Australia the world's eighth-highest marginal tax rate, compared with 33 per cent in New Zealand, 20 per cent in Singapore and 15 per cent in Hong Kong.

Argued that Labor would not block the Tax Laws Amendment (Temporary Budget Repair Levy) Bill 2014, but cited NATSEM modelling showing the poorest 20 per cent of families, earning less than $35,000 a year after tax, will lose almost five per cent of disposable income, versus a 0.2 per cent loss for the top 20 per cent earning $88,000 or more.

Argued against the broader budget package while not opposing the levy itself, said his Fowler electorate has an average personal income of about $20,000 and an average household income of $55,000, well below the $180,000 threshold at which the new levy applies.

Argued that the poorest bear the heaviest burden in this budget, citing modelling that a young jobseeker earning just over $13,000 a year will lose almost $7,000, and said about 30 per cent of her Bendigo electorate survives on less than $600 a week.

Explained that the Tax Laws Amendment (Temporary Budget Repair Levy) Bill 2014 introduces a three-year, two per cent levy on taxable income above $180,000, starting in the 2014 to 2015 financial year, and accused the Prime Minister of promising no new taxes before the election then introducing this levy afterward.

Argued that the Tax Laws Amendment (Temporary Budget Repair Levy) Bill 2014 exposes the Prime Minister's broken tax promises, quoting his pre-election pledges that there would be tax cuts without new taxes, no new tax collection without an election, and that personal income tax would be lower under a coalition government.
Tax Laws Amendment (Temporary Budget Repair Levy) Act 2014

Introduced a bill amending the Migration Act in response to recent Federal Court and High Court rulings, clarifying when a visa decision is finally determined, restoring a bar on repeat protection visa applications on different grounds, and reinstating a criterion requiring applicants not be assessed by ASIO as a security risk.

The Selection of Bills Committee presented its 11th report of 2013, recommending six bills be referred to specific committees for inquiry with set reporting dates, including the Environment Legislation Amendment Bill 2013 (report by 12 February 2014) and the Criminal Code Amendment (Harming Australians) Bill 2013 (report by 4 March 2014).

Announced Labor's support for the Migration Amendment Bill 2013, which clarifies when a protection visa decision is finally made, bars repeat applications on new grounds after a failed claim, and blocks a protection visa for anyone with a negative ASIO security assessment, while noting the Stone review process remains intact.

Announced Labor's support for the Migration Amendment Bill 2013, citing the Federal Court's 2012 SZQOY decision and its 11 September 2013 SZRNY judgement on when a protection visa review decision becomes final, and the SZGIZ case on repeat applications.

Opposed the Migration Amendment Bill 2013 on behalf of the Greens, arguing it denies refugees the right to know or challenge adverse ASIO security assessments, and cited a UN Human Rights Committee finding that Australia committed 143 human rights violations by indefinitely detaining 46 refugees, including children.

Summed up the Migration Amendment Bill 2013 as the responsible minister, describing schedules that clarify when protection visa decisions are finalised, close a loophole allowing repeat applications identified in the SZGIZ Federal Court case, and address the High Court's M47/2012 ruling on ASIO security assessments, noting the department employs over 10,000 staff.
This bill aims to improve how registered organisations like unions and employer groups are run and overseen.
It would set up a new independent body called the Registered Organisations Commission with stronger investigation powers.
Penalties would rise and new criminal offences would apply for serious misconduct by officers, mirroring rules for company directors.
Establishes the Registered Organisations Commission as an independent regulator.
Strengthens financial reporting and transparency rules by making some obligations enforceable as civil remedy provisions.
Increases civil penalties and creates criminal offences for serious breaches of officers' duties.
Expands disclosure requirements for officers' material personal interests and changes grounds for disqualification from office.
Gives the Commissioner investigation and information-gathering powers modelled on those in the Australian Securities and Investments Commission Act 2001.
Registered organisations, their branches, and their officers.

Introduced a bill establishing a Registered Organisations Commission modelled on the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, citing Craig Thomson facing more than 150 fraud related charges and Michael Williamson pleading guilty to misusing almost $1 million of Health Services Union funds, and raising maximum penalties from 60 penalty units to 1,200 for individuals and 6,000 for a body corporate.

Opposed the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2013, arguing the government has not proven current regulation is failing after Labor tripled penalties last year, and cited employer group submissions warning the bill imposes obligations more onerous than the Corporations Act 2001 requires of company directors.

Supported the bill, arguing the Health Services Union scandal involving Craig Thomson and Michael Williamson showed existing regulation of registered organisations is inadequate, and welcomed the new Registered Organisations Commission's stronger investigation and disclosure powers to prevent similar misconduct.

Opposed the bill, arguing that the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Act 2012 already strengthened regulation and that unions differ fundamentally from for-profit corporations, cited the Australian Industry Group's view that the disclosure rules are unfair to non-profit organisations, and called for the bill to be referred to the Senate references committee.

Supported the bill, arguing that the Health Services Union scandal, which involved nearly $1 million of members' funds, shows the need for the new Registered Organisations Commission with stronger, ASIC-style investigation powers, and noted that Bill Shorten's own bill had been given only five days of Senate committee scrutiny.

Supported the bill, arguing it will reassure workers that their union contributions cannot be misappropriated after the Thomson affair and the Health Services Union scandal, and noted that Fair Work Australia's registered organisations include employer bodies such as the Australian Education Union, not only trade unions.

Opposed the bill, said the Independent Education Union raised fees by two per cent to meet compliance costs under similar legislation already introduced by Campbell Newman in Queensland, and objected that executive members would have to register even their young children's Dollarmite bank accounts as personal interests.

Supported the bill, arguing that unions and employer bodies control large sums, illustrated by a leadership contest for the Queensland branch of the Transport Workers Union that oversaw about $11 million in assets, with $500,000 reportedly spent to change its leadership, showing the need for stronger financial oversight.

A motion to refer the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2013 to the Education and Employment References Committee was proposed on behalf of Senator Wong but was blocked by an objection.

The motion to refer the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2013 to the Education and Employment References Committee was moved, arguing that the bill was rushed with only one day of public hearings and that further scrutiny was needed, while opponents cited the government's election mandate and the need for higher penalties for union officials, referencing Justice North's criticism of existing penalties and the support of figures like Paul Howes.

Opposed the Fair Work Registered Organisations Amendment Bill, noted the unusual alignment of both the Australian Industry Group and unions in calling for more time to consider it, and accused the government of failing Holden workers and axing a fund meant to raise early childhood educators' wages.

Opposed the bill, tracing the coalition's industrial relations approach back to the Howard government's 2004 Senate takeover and Work Choices, said Labor's 2012 reforms had already tripled penalties for union misconduct following the Health Services Union scandal, and noted the National Workplace Relations Consultative Council itself had recommended the bill be delayed for further consultation.

Opposed the bill and called for Senate committee referral, noted Labor's 2012 reforms had already tripled penalties for registered organisation misconduct, cited the Australian Industry Group's submission that its 78 unpaid councillors would face disclosure requirements exceeding those on well-paid company directors, and said some proposed penalties would increase by two-thirds or more beyond existing law.

Opposed the bill, said the current Fair Work registered organisations framework, introduced in 2009 and strengthened in 2012, already imposes tough penalties, criticised new criminal penalties of up to $340,000 or five years imprisonment as unnecessary duplication of existing law, and noted a government member mentioned unions 25 times in one speech despite denying the bill targeted them.
The speaker tabled additional information from inquiries into amendments to the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2013 and the effectiveness of NAPLAN.

The speaker moved a motion to change committee memberships, discharging Senator Urquhart and appointing Senator Gallacher to the National Disability Insurance Scheme Joint Standing Committee, and appointing substitute members for several other committees including Wright, Milne, and Ludlam.

Closed debate on the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2013, citing HSU and other union slush fund scandals to justify establishing an independent Registered Organisations Commission with stronger investigative powers and higher civil and criminal penalties aligned with the Corporations Act, and noted the Senate Standing Committee on Education and Employment's report tabled on 2 December.

Opposed the bill reviving the Australian Building and Construction Commission, said the 2001 Cole royal commission cost $66 million over 18 months without producing a single criminal conviction, criticised the bill for denying workers the right to silence and legal representation in secret interviews, and noted a former Federal Court judge had previously described the consulting firm's productivity modelling underpinning the bill as deeply flawed.

Moved a debate management motion capping the Minerals Resource Rent Tax Repeal and Other Measures Bill's second reading debate and limiting consideration in detail to 60 minutes, defending it as routine scheduling and noting the House was waiting to hear the member for Banks give his maiden speech.

Opposed the bill repealing the mining tax and other measures, comparing it to opposition raised against the Hawke government's petroleum resource rent tax, which has since raised $39 billion, and criticised the retrospective abolition of the low income superannuation contribution for people earning under $37,000 while high-income superannuation tax breaks remain.

Opposed the bill's abolition of the schoolkids bonus, the income support bonus and the low income superannuation contribution, saying 1.3 million families and 2.2 million children would be worse off, and that families could lose up to $15,000 over their children's schooling.

Defended the profits-based mining tax, citing Treasury's own costings showing its repeal would cost the budget around $4 billion, noted mining exploration spending rose from $5.7 billion in 2009-10 to $7.8 billion in 2012-13 despite the tax, and quoted evidence that Fortescue Metals Group had not yet paid any corporate tax.

Supported repealing the mining tax as a clear election commitment, argued mining resources belong to the states rather than the Commonwealth, and accused the former Labor government of fostering entitlement, recalling that Kevin Rudd's 2007 election promise of a Western Australian infrastructure fund was never delivered.

Supported repealing the mining tax, noting it raised only about $400 million against $16.7 billion in committed spending over the forward estimates, and said Australia has gone from $60 billion in surplus in 2007 to $292 billion in debt, criticising the schoolkids bonus payments of $800 and $400 as an unfunded handout.

Opposed the mining tax repeal bill, warning it scraps the low-income superannuation contribution of up to $500 for workers earning under $37,000, affecting 2.1 million women, delays the super guarantee rise to 12 per cent at a cost of $53 billion in national savings by 2021 to 2022, and cuts the schoolkids bonus of $410 and $820 per student for 1.3 million families.

Opposed repealing the mining tax, warning the abolition of the Regional Infrastructure Fund leaves many projects with no confirmed funding, and quoted a 2011 speech criticising mining companies for investing little back into the communities whose resources they extract, before revealing the quote came from the now Deputy Prime Minister.

Supported repealing the mining tax, criticising the Regional Development Australia Fund for committing $916 million, or 95 per cent, of its $952 million allocation by election time, including $608 million in the final three and a half months, and said Australia had accumulated $300 billion in debt in six years under the previous government.

Opposed repealing the mining tax, defending the schoolkids bonus of $410 and $820 per student for 1.3 million families, criticising the delay to raising the super guarantee from nine to 12 per cent, and citing estimates that scrapping the low-income superannuation contribution would cut national savings by $53 billion by 2021.

Opposed the bill, arguing that repealing the minerals resource rent tax would remove the schoolkids bonus, low-income superannuation support, the income support bonus and small-business tax concessions, while increasing taxes on low-paid workers and reducing investment in infrastructure.

Supported the bill, arguing that repealing the minerals resource rent tax would improve the budget bottom line by $15 billion over the current forward estimates, restore investor confidence, reduce compliance costs and benefit Western Australia's mining and regional sectors.

Opposed the bill, arguing that the minerals resource rent tax fairly shared mining superprofits with Australians and funded support for families, low-income workers, small businesses and mining-affected regions, while its repeal would benefit large mining companies at others' expense.
Argued that mineral resources belong to the states, supporting the principle underlying state royalty provisions.

Opposed the bill, arguing that it would benefit three large multinational mining companies while removing or delaying support for families, small businesses and retirement savings, including the planned increase in compulsory superannuation contributions from nine to 12 per cent.

Supported repealing the minerals resource rent tax, arguing that it was poorly implemented, discouraged foreign investment and harmed growth, jobs and regional Australia, while the coalition was fulfilling its 7 September election mandate.

Supported repealing the Minerals Resource Rent Tax, arguing one company told him it could cost up to $7 million just to collect and remit the tax, more than it delivered in revenue, while conceding a case might exist for retaining a profits-based tax on foreign-owned iron ore or coal miners.

Supported repealing the Minerals Resource Rent Tax, citing stalled Queensland coal projects including Waratah Coal's 4,400 million tonne Galilee Basin discovery and Glencore Xstrata's Wandoan project, and said the tax was predicted to raise $26.5 billion over five years but had collected only four hundred million dollars.

Opened his summation of debate on the Minerals Resource Rent Tax repeal bill, criticising the shadow Treasurer's contribution as failing to appreciate the damage caused by the tax and containing several inaccuracies about its operation.

Defended the Minerals Resource Rent Tax Repeal and Other Measures Bill 2013, arguing the government's cuts are necessary because Labor's spending left Australia with more than $400 billion in debt and the five biggest budget deficits in the nation's history.

This division relates to the Policies _[For a carbon price](/policies/3)_ and _[For renewable energy](/policies/20)_. The majority voted in favour of a [motion](http://www.openaustralia.org/senate/?gid=2013-12-02.129.1) that: _At the end of the motion that the resumption of debate be made an order of debate for a later hour add: 'and the orders of the day for the resumption of the second reading debate on the Clean Energy Finance Corporation (Abolition) Bill 2013, and subsequently the Climate Change Authority (Abolition) Bill 2013, have precedence over this bill and the other related bills until determined.'_ (You can read the associated debate [here](http://www.openaustralia.org/senate/?id=2013-12-02.127.1). It commenced after 8:38 pm. ) Passing this motion means that the second reading debate about the Clean Energy Finance Corporation (Abolition) Bill 2013 and the Climate Change Authority (Abolition) Bill 2013 will be resumed before the debate about the Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013 and other related bills. The motion was introduced by Labor Senator [Penny Wong](http://publicwhip-rails.openaustraliafoundation.org.au/mp.php?mpn=Penny_Wong&mpc=Senate&house=senate). _Background to the bills_ The Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013 was introduced into Parliament as part of a package of eleven bills to remove the [carbon pricing mechanism](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_pricing_in_Australia) and abolish the [Clean Energy Finance Corporation](http://www.cleanenergyfinancecorp.com.au/about-us.aspx) and the [Climate Change Authority](http://climatechangeauthority.gov.au/about). The eleven bills are: - [Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r5137) - [True-up Shortfall Levy (General) (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r5131)
Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013 and related bills - Second Reading - Protect Australia from climate change

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](http://www.openaustralia.org/senate/?gid=2014-03-17.17.1) introduced by Labor Senator [Jacinta Collins](http://publicwhip-rails.openaustraliafoundation.org.au/mp.php?mpn=Jacinta_Collins&mpc=Senate&house=senate). The motion was for an amendment to be added to the end of the original motion, which was "_That these bills be now read a second time._" The words were: "_but the Senate calls on the Government to recognise the scientific expert consensus regarding [climate change](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change) and that the repeal of the carbon tax must be accompanied by the introduction of serious and comprehensive policies to address climate change._" Since the motion passed, these words will now be added to the original motion. Background to the bills The [Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r5137) and related bills were introduced as a package to remove the [carbon pricing mechanism](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_pricing_in_Australia), which was introduced by the Australian Labor Party while in government. The Coalition described the mechanism as a “carbon tax” and removing it was a key policy platform during the 2013 election.(You can read more about the Coalition's policy to remove the carbon price [here](http://www.liberal.org.au/scrapping-carbon-tax-and-reducing-cost-living). ) The carbon pricing mechanism commenced on 1 July 2012.(For more information on the carbon pricing mechanism and how it works, please see the Clean Energy Regulator’s [website](http://www.cleanenergyregulator.gov.au/Carbon-Pricing-Mechanism/About-the-Mechanism/Pages/default.aspx).) It is an emissions trading scheme that puts a price on carbon emissions. It applies to “liable entities” (a group that includes companies that emit a high level of greenhouse gases). Moved the second reading of a bill imposing a true-up shortfall levy to recover overallocated assistance under the Jobs and Competitiveness Program, ensuring businesses are not over- or under-compensated in the 2013 to 2014 financial year.

Moved the second reading of a related bill imposing an excise-based true-up shortfall levy to recover the value of overallocated free carbon units issued under the Jobs and Competitiveness Program for the 2013 to 2014 financial year.

Moved a debate management motion to conclude debate on the Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013 and related bills by Thursday this week, arguing the election gave the coalition a mandate with 90 seats to Labor's 55, Labor's worst result since 1903.

Argued against the government's carbon tax repeal bills, saying the decade from 2001 to 2010 was the warmest on record, that Direct Action would cost households an estimated $1,200 a year without a legislated cap on emissions, and noted that under Labor wind power generation trebled and 24,000 renewable energy jobs were created.

Continued opposing the carbon tax repeal bills, saying NASA had confirmed 97 per cent of actively publishing climate scientists agree human activity causes global warming, cited the IPCC's Fifth Assessment Report finding 95 per cent certainty on human-caused climate change, and noted global average surface temperatures had risen by almost 0.9 degrees Celsius since 1880.

Supported repealing the carbon tax, saying Sydney households had faced a 57 per cent increase in power bills since 2010, and noted Australia's $25 a tonne carbon price was the highest in the world with no other country imposing an economy-wide carbon tax.

Supported repealing the carbon tax, citing a 15.3 per cent rise in electricity prices in the first quarter after its introduction and an almost 11 per cent swing to the Liberal Party in his Bass electorate at the 2013 election, and said the tax cost the economy $9 billion.

Opposed repealing the carbon tax, citing a $4.4 million grant that cut the JBS meatworks' carbon price liability by $790,000 a year in his Ipswich electorate, and said the coalition's review had put a $1.2 million LED street lighting grant for Ipswich in jeopardy.

Argued that the Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013 would fulfil the coalition's promise to repeal the carbon tax, restore trust and reduce costs, while claiming the tax disadvantaged Australian businesses, consumers and jobs and had negligible effects on global temperatures.

Argued that emissions trading would burden Australia's coal and aluminium industries, questioned who would benefit from it, and advocated ethanol as a way to reduce transport emissions, citing international use and potential reductions from grain and sugarcane ethanol.

Supported repealing the Clean Energy Act 2011 and associated charges acts, abolishing related assistance and institutions, and using the ACCC to ensure prices fell, arguing the carbon tax harmed households, businesses and jobs and that the election endorsed repeal.

Argued for repealing the carbon tax, citing Alcoa's warning that the tax would cost Australian aluminium producers at least $60 a tonne while its Western Australian refineries had already cut emissions per tonne by more than 20 per cent since 1990 without one, and noted Western Power's own trigger point for changing behaviour was $90 a tonne.
Argued for repealing the carbon tax, citing about 13,000 small businesses in Calare and an example of a $10,000 annual electricity bill rising by $1,000 a year because of the tax.

Opposed repealing the carbon tax, arguing the science of climate change is settled and defending the scheme's three-year fixed price period, and noted Australia's carbon price has worked since 1 July 2012, comparing it to California's emissions trading scheme covering about 60 per cent of its economy since 1 January 2013 and China's new carbon pricing trials in seven provinces.

Supported repealing the carbon tax, citing government modelling that the carbon price was set to reach $56 a tonne, said scrapping it would leave average households $550 a year better off from 2014 to 2015, and cited an Australian Industry Group survey of 485 businesses that found manufacturing energy costs rose by an average of 14.5 per cent because of the tax.

Argued that most electricity price rises in New South Wales stemmed from state network costs rather than the carbon price, said Direct Action modelling showed it would cost Australian households $1,200, and quoted Malcolm Turnbull's December 2009 criticism of the then Opposition Leader's shifting positions on emissions trading, alongside 97 per cent scientific agreement on climate change.

Recalled then Prime Minister Gillard's 2010 promise of no carbon tax before it was legislated on 11 October 2012, cited local business examples in the Higgins electorate of sharp bill increases attributed to a 'carbon charge', and said Treasury modelling showed repeal would save households around $550 a year.

Supported the bill to reduce Territory bills and argued that the carbon tax should be repealed, saying it increased costs for households, businesses and local government without delivering environmental benefits. Cited Treasury modelling of an average household cost reduction of around $550 during the 2014-15 financial year and urged Territory representatives to support repeal.

Opposed the Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013, citing a 6.1 per cent drop in electricity sector emissions equivalent to 12 million tonnes of carbon dioxide, a 30 per cent surge in renewable energy generation, and more than 150,000 jobs created since the carbon price began.

Supported repealing the carbon tax, arguing it had raised $16 billion over two years without reducing domestic emissions, promised families would be $550 a year better off once it is scrapped, and confirmed the government retains the same five per cent emissions reduction target by 2020 that Labor had set.

Opposed repealing the carbon tax, noting that sixty-odd thousand Australians attended climate change rallies around the country on the weekend, including firefighters concerned about the impact on their work, and argued the government's course of cutting the Clean Energy Finance Corporation and scientists' funding is the wrong direction.
